tagline: The book of beginnings: God makes a good world, humanity breaks it, and God promises to bless every nation through one family.
overview:
Genesis is the first book of the Bible and the first of the five books of the Torah, the Law of Moses, also called the Pentateuch. Its English name comes through the Septuagint (the Greek translation of the Hebrew Scriptures made from the third century BC onward) and means origin or birth. In Hebrew the book is called Bereshit, its opening word, which means in the beginning. That is exactly what it offers: the beginning of the world, of human beings, of marriage and work, of sin and death, of nations and languages, and of the people of Israel.

The book moves in two great sweeps. Chapters 1 to 11 tell the story of the whole world: God creates the heavens and the earth and makes humanity in his image; the first couple disobey and are sent out of Eden; Cain murders Abel; violence fills the earth until God sends the flood and starts again with Noah; and humanity gathers at Babel to make a name for itself and is scattered. Chapters 12 to 50 narrow to one family. God calls Abraham, promises him descendants, a land, and a blessing that will reach all the families of the earth, and then follows that promise through Isaac, through Jacob (renamed Israel) and his twelve sons, and finally through Joseph, whose brothers sell him into slavery and who rises to save Egypt and his own family from famine.

The rest of the Bible stands on this book. Its account of God as sole creator, of every person as bearing his image, of sin as a rupture between people and God, and of God's covenant promise to Abraham is assumed on almost every later page. Genesis ends with the family living in Egypt and Joseph's body in a coffin, waiting to be carried home. The promise is alive, but it is not yet kept, and the reader turns to Exodus to see what God will do.
author:
Genesis never names its author. Jewish and Christian tradition has long credited the five books of the Torah to Moses, and the New Testament speaks of these books as the law of Moses. Because Genesis describes events centuries before Moses was born, those who hold to his authorship usually say he worked from older records and oral traditions, and some suggest that the book's recurring headings (This is the account of...) mark such earlier sources. A few details show at least some later updating, which many conservative scholars readily accept: Genesis 14:14 mentions the city of Dan, a name the town received only in the period of the judges (Judges 18:29), and Genesis 36:31 lists Edomite kings who reigned before any king reigned over Israel, a remark that assumes Israel's monarchy.

Most critical scholars since the late nineteenth century have seen the Pentateuch as a combination of several sources. The classic form of this theory, the Documentary Hypothesis associated with Julius Wellhausen, identified four documents written at different times and later woven together, two of which appear in Genesis as a strand that prefers the divine name LORD and a priestly strand concerned with genealogies, covenants, and order. Since the 1970s that model has been heavily revised, and many scholars now speak more simply of priestly and non-priestly material, with debate over how and when they were joined. Other scholars stress the book's unified design and argue that it is better explained as the deliberate work of one author or editor using older material. Readers across these views agree that Genesis as we have it is a carefully shaped whole.
date:
The date of writing depends on the question of authorship. On the traditional view Genesis comes from the time of Moses, which places it in either the fifteenth or the thirteenth century BC, depending on how one dates the exodus (itself a contested question, with some reading 1 Kings 6:1 to place it around 1446 BC and others preferring a thirteenth-century date on archaeological grounds). Critical scholars generally date its sources between the tenth and sixth centuries BC and place the final shaping of the book in the Persian period, after the return from Babylonian exile that followed Cyrus's decree in 539/538 BC.

The events themselves are a separate question. Chapters 1 to 11 give no dates that can be tied to known history. The stories of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob have traditionally been placed in the early second millennium BC, roughly 2000 to 1700 BC, and Joseph's rise in Egypt somewhat later. Since the 1970s a number of scholars have argued that the patriarchal stories reflect conditions of the first millennium BC and preserve little reliable memory of an earlier age, while others continue to argue that they fit the earlier period well. The book itself shows more interest in what God promised than in dates.
setting:
Genesis moves across the whole ancient Near East. Its first chapters look toward Mesopotamia, the land between the Tigris and Euphrates rivers, where the Sumerians and later the Babylonians built some of the world's first cities. Abraham's family comes from Ur and Harran in that region. The central chapters take place in Canaan, the land between the Jordan River and the Mediterranean, a patchwork of small city-states where the patriarchs lived as outsiders, moving their flocks between towns, digging wells, and negotiating with local rulers. The last chapters are set in Egypt, the great kingdom of the Nile, whose grain could feed its neighbors when rain failed in Canaan.

Those neighboring cultures had their own stories of beginnings. The Babylonian Enuma Elish tells of creation through a war among the gods. The Atrahasis epic tells of the gods making humans to do their labor and then sending a flood when people became too many and too noisy. The Epic of Gilgamesh includes a flood hero named Utnapishtim who builds a boat and sends out birds. The Sumerian King List names kings who reigned for thousands of years before a flood. Genesis shares some of this world's questions and imagery, but it answers them with one God, a good creation, and human beings made for dignity rather than drudgery. The first readers, whether Israel in the wilderness after Egypt or Israel in the long aftermath of exile in Babylon, needed to hear exactly that difference.
purpose: Genesis tells Israel who its God is and why it exists. It shows that the LORD who called Abraham is no local deity but the maker of heaven and earth, that the world's brokenness comes from human rebellion rather than from the nature of things, and that God answered that rebellion not by abandoning the world but by choosing one family through whom he would bless all the others. It explains why Israel had a claim to the land of Canaan, why it traced its tribes to twelve brothers, and how it came to be in Egypt, which sets the stage for the exodus. For any later reader, it answers the oldest questions about where we came from, what we are for, what went wrong, and whether God has given up on us.
story: Genesis is where the story begins, so nothing comes before it except God himself. Everything after it depends on it. Exodus opens with Jacob's descendants multiplying in Egypt, becoming slaves, and being rescued, which is the first great fulfillment of the promise that Abraham's offspring would become a nation. The covenant at Sinai, the entry into the land under Joshua, and the kingdom of David each carry forward the promises of offspring, land, and blessing made in Genesis 12 to 22. The exile seems to undo them, and the prophets look beyond it to a new start. The New Testament presents Jesus as the one in whom those promises are finally kept, and the Bible's last chapters return to images from Genesis 2, a river of life and the tree of life, in a new creation where the curse is gone.
christ:
The New Testament reads Genesis as the opening of the story that Christ completes. After the first sin God tells the serpent that the woman's seed will crush its head (Genesis 3:15). Christian readers since at least the second century, Irenaeus among them, have heard in this the first announcement of the gospel, while many modern interpreters read it first as a promise of humanity's long struggle with evil; Paul echoes it when he writes, “The God of peace will soon crush Satan under your feet” (Romans 16:20). Paul calls Adam “a pattern of the One to come” (Romans 5:14), the first head of humanity whose failure Christ reverses.

The promise to Abraham is the book's backbone, and Paul says that in it God “foretold the gospel to Abraham” (Galatians 3:8). He reads the promised seed as fulfilled in Christ (Galatians 3:16), and he holds up Abraham, who believed God and was counted righteous (Genesis 15:6), as the model of faith for Jew and Gentile alike (Romans 4). Hebrews finds in Melchizedek, the priest-king of Salem, a pattern for Christ's priesthood (Hebrews 7), and in Abraham's offering of Isaac a faith that expected God to raise the dead (Hebrews 11:17-19). Other links are patterns rather than predictions: Judah's scepter in Genesis 49:10 was read by later Jewish and Christian interpreters as a royal hope, and Joseph, rejected by his brothers and then raised up to save them, has long been seen as a picture of the rejected and exalted Christ.
reading: Genesis is narrative, with poetry at key moments (2:23, 3:14-19, 49) and genealogies that serve as its skeleton rather than filler. Watch for the recurring heading, This is the account of..., which opens each new section, and for the patterns the book repeats: the younger son preferred over the older, barren wives who conceive only by God's intervention, a patriarch passing off his wife as his sister (chapters 12, 20, and 26), and blessings and curses spoken over children. The narrator rarely stops to pass moral judgment, so describing an act is not the same as approving it; the consequences usually do the judging. Two misreadings are common. One treats the patriarchs as moral heroes to copy, when the book presents them as flawed people carried by a faithful God. The other reduces chapters 1 to 11 to a question of science versus myth. Readers differ on how literally to take those chapters, but the book's own concern is who God is, who we are, and how God keeps his word.

structure.title: The seven days of creation
structure.summary: God creates the heavens and the earth by his word, makes humanity in his image, calls everything very good, and rests on the seventh day.

structure.title: From Eden to Babel
structure.summary: The first couple in the garden, their disobedience and exile, Cain's murder of Abel, the flood and God's covenant with Noah, the table of nations, and the scattering at Babel. Sin spreads, and God keeps preserving and judging.

structure.title: Abraham
structure.summary: God calls Abram out of Mesopotamia and promises him offspring, land, and blessing for all nations. Through long waiting, failure, and testing, the promised son Isaac is born and Abraham dies owning only a burial plot in Canaan.

structure.title: Isaac, Jacob, and Esau
structure.summary: Jacob grasps the blessing from his brother, flees to Harran, builds a family of twelve sons amid rivalry, wrestles with God and is renamed Israel, and returns to the land. Esau's line becomes Edom.

structure.title: Joseph and his brothers
structure.summary: Joseph is sold into Egypt by his brothers, rises from prison to rule under Pharaoh, and saves the family from famine. Reconciled, the brothers settle in Egypt, Jacob blesses his sons, and Joseph dies trusting God to bring them home.

themes.title: Blessing and curse
themes.body: God's first word to humanity is a blessing (1:28), and sin brings curse on the serpent and the ground (3:14-17), on Cain (4:11), and on Canaan (9:25). The call of Abraham answers that spread of curse with a fivefold repetition of blessing (12:1-3). The rest of the book traces who receives the blessing, how it is passed on, and how it reaches outsiders such as Laban and Potiphar and finally Pharaoh and all Egypt through Joseph.

themes.title: The promised offspring
themes.body: The word seed, or offspring, runs from 3:15 through the promises to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. Yet the promise keeps meeting obstacles: barren wives, murdered sons, famine, a father told to sacrifice his heir, brothers who try to kill one of their own. Genesis shows that the line of promise survives because God preserves it, not because the family is strong or good.

themes.title: The land
themes.body: God promises Abraham the land of Canaan, but Abraham lives in it as a foreigner and owns only a cave for a grave (chapter 23). Jacob spends twenty years away from it and his sons end the book in Egypt. The land is promised, walked through, and longed for, and Joseph's final request to have his bones carried there leaves the promise pointing forward into Exodus and Joshua.

themes.title: God's choice of the unlikely
themes.body: Again and again God passes over the expected heir: Abel and then Seth rather than Cain, Isaac rather than Ishmael, Jacob rather than Esau, Joseph and Judah rather than Reuben, Ephraim rather than Manasseh. The pattern overturns the ancient assumption that the firstborn inherits by right and shows that God's purposes rest on his free choice and grace.

themes.title: Providence through human failure
themes.body: The people of Genesis lie, scheme, play favorites, and betray one another, and God works through all of it without excusing any of it. The theme comes to its clearest statement at the end, when Joseph tells his brothers that what they intended for evil God intended for good (50:20). Genesis teaches that God's plan is not derailed by human sin, which is both a comfort and a warning.

keyChapters.why: God creates the world by his word and makes humanity, male and female, in his image. The foundation of the Bible's teaching on God, creation, and human dignity.
The first disobedience, its consequences, and the first hint of hope in the promise about the woman's seed. Everything that goes wrong in the Bible's story traces back here.
After the flood God makes a covenant with Noah and every living creature, promising never again to destroy the earth by flood, and grounds the value of human life in the image of God.
God calls Abram and promises him a great nation, a great name, and blessing for all the families of the earth. The hinge on which the whole Bible turns from the world's story to Israel's.
Abram believes the LORD and it is credited to him as righteousness, and God binds himself by covenant in a strange night ceremony. Paul builds his teaching on faith on this chapter.
God tests Abraham by commanding him to offer Isaac, then provides a ram in his place. One of the most searching and most discussed stories in Scripture.
Jacob wrestles through the night with a mysterious man, is renamed Israel, and walks away limping and blessed. The nation takes its name from this encounter.
Joseph forgives his brothers and names God's providence over their evil, and he dies trusting God to bring Israel back to the promised land.
